answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the current revision of the GHG Protocol standards.

Dow strongly supports the inclusion of market-based mechanisms across all scopes, provided these are paired with clear guidance to ensure scientific integrity and consistency in corporate GHG inventories and product carbon footprint standards. There is a critical need for the updated GHG Protocol to clearly differentiate between attributional and consequential accounting for market instruments, and to establish transparent rules regarding how such instruments are incorporated into corporate and product GHG accounting. Attributional approaches allocate climate attributes to products or activities, while consequential approaches measure impacts resulting from specific interventions. Both methodologies offer value but serve distinct purposes, and Dow believes that they must be clearly defined and reported separately without ambiguity to uphold scientific integrity and advance value chain decarbonization.

Additionally, Dow encourages the Protocol to expand its definition of physical connectivity, for example with aspects of the AMI quality criteria. In today’s global production networks and supply chains, climate attributes are not inherently linked to individual physical molecules. As such, Dow contends that strict point-to-point traceability should not be mandated where it does not meaningfully enhance accuracy. Instead, physical connectivity can be appropriately defined at the level of an activity pool or supply shed, that is, the set of emission sources that may physically serve a reporting entity, even if further traceability to a specific facility is not feasible. Within these boundaries, credible mass-balance or book-and-claim systems can be implemented, provided they include safeguards such as technical feasibility, mass-energy constraints, residual product mix checks, and transparent attribution mechanisms, specifically within corporate boundaries.

Dow believes that these market-based decarbonization approaches, when supported by rigorous guardrails, are consistent with the GHG inventory framework for corporate accounting and can facilitate more accurate supplier-specific data while accelerating real emissions reductions across value chains.
